title: India Pulls In $20 Billion From Diaspora, but Oil Surge Keeps Rupee Pinned Near Record Low
excerpt: India's push to attract dollar deposits from overseas Indians has drawn over $20 billion in a month, yet the rupee continues to weaken as surging oil prices and an internal RBI debate on intervention strategy compound currency pressures.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India attracted over $20 billion in diaspora deposits, yet the rupee remains near record lows.
  • Brent crude oil prices surged above $96 per barrel, intensifying pressure on India's economy.
  • The RBI faces internal conflict over currency intervention strategies, causing market uncertainty.
  • In May, the RBI sold $6.1 billion in forex markets, with reserves declining to $675.2 billion.

India's ambitious bid to tap its overseas population for dollar inflows has drawn more than $20 billion in about a month, according to Reuters — an impressive haul that has nonetheless failed to arrest the rupee's slide toward record lows.

The currency traded at 96.48 per dollar on Thursday, up a marginal 0.1% from the previous session after touching its weakest level in over two months the day before. The rupee has shed nearly 2% in July alone, the worst showing among Asian peers, erasing a June recovery driven by earlier oil price declines and the very deposit incentives now proving insufficient.

Oil Prices Overwhelm Diaspora Dollars

The core problem is crude oil. Brent has surged above $96 a barrel to its highest level in six weeks after the United States launched a 12th consecutive night of strikes on Iran-linked targets and Yemen's Houthis targeted oil tankers in the Red Sea, including vessels carrying Saudi crude.

“It is difficult to see any meaningful relief for the rupee if oil prices keep moving higher like this. The risk of Brent crossing the $100 mark and moving higher is increasing.”

— Currency trader at a private-sector bank, via Reuters

India imports nearly 90% of its crude oil, making higher energy prices a triple threat: they slow growth, lift inflation, and widen the current account deficit. Analysts at MUFG warned that disruptions to Gulf oil shipments, combined with rising US Treasury yields, are “likely to weigh broadly on Asian currencies,” with the key risk being whether the conflict triggers “a broader global energy shock.”

The RBI's Internal Tug of War

Compounding the rupee's woes is a policy vacuum at the Reserve Bank of India. Three sources familiar with the central bank's internal discussions told Reuters that officials are split on how aggressively to defend the currency.

Governor Malhotra and Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta — both external appointees — favour letting the market largely determine the exchange rate, intervening only to curb excessive volatility. They believe the currency should adjust to macroeconomic realities, including a heavier oil import bill, the sources said.

That view clashes with RBI veterans involved in market operations, who advocate more regular, forceful intervention to discourage one-way bets against the rupee. The result has been confusion among traders, who expected stronger support after Malhotra publicly pledged to do “whatever is required” to ensure orderly currency moves.

The data underscores the scale of past intervention. The RBI sold a net $6.1 billion in forex markets in May alone — purchasing $22.2 billion and selling $28.3 billion — after net sales of $8.9 billion in April. Its net outstanding forward dollar sales hit a record $106.6 billion by end-May, up from $95.3 billion a month earlier.

Foreign exchange reserves have declined to $675.2 billion from a peak of $728.5 billion in March. Some analysts peg usable reserves — after stripping out gold holdings and forward commitments — at roughly $460 billion.

Diaspora Scheme: Big Numbers, Bigger Ambitions

Oil Price Surge Impact
›Brent crude oil price exceeds $96 per barrel.
›India imports nearly 90% of its crude oil.
›Higher oil prices threaten growth and increase inflation.
›Potential for Brent to cross $100 mark.

The $20 billion raised so far stems from an RBI scheme launched in June that absorbs the cost of hedging foreign-currency deposits placed with Indian banks for three to five years. The arrangement lets overseas Indians earn domestic interest rates of 6% to 7% without bearing currency risk — a structure banks have marketed aggressively.

Analysts see room for much more. Nomura estimates the scheme could attract roughly $55 billion, while Axis Bank projects potential inflows as high as $100 billion. With leverage via dollar loans — which banks are seeking RBI approval to offer — returns could approach 12% to 15%, according to Macquarie and Axis estimates respectively.

“Disruptions to oil shipments from the Gulf, combined with rising US Treasury yields, are likely to weigh broadly on Asian currencies.”

— MUFG analysts, in a research note

India was the world's largest remittance recipient in 2024, taking in nearly $138 billion, according to the International Organization for Migration. The US has overtaken the UAE as the top source of inward remittances, accounting for 27.7% of flows in FY24, reflecting a structural shift toward white-collar diaspora earnings.

What Comes Next

RBI's Intervention Dilemma
›Split views within RBI on currency intervention.
›Governor favors market-led approach.
›Record $106.6 billion in forward dollar sales.
›Traders uncertain about RBI's policy direction.

The outlook hinges on two variables: oil and the RBI's willingness to burn reserves. Foreign investors have net purchased about $4.5 billion of Indian government bonds over June and July, offering some support. But two Singapore-based hedge fund managers told Reuters they have reinstated bearish rupee positions after the currency broke through levels they expected the RBI to defend.

If Brent sustains above $96 and the central bank continues its softer intervention posture, traders say the rupee could retest its all-time low of 96.96 — a level it first touched in May — in the near term. The diaspora dollars, while meaningful, cannot on their own offset the daily structural demand for dollars from Indian oil refiners paying a higher import bill.
